This disease differs from other causes of HCM in that it tends to be inherited within families. The mutations are found in genes encoding proteins involved in the excitation-contraction coupling of muscle cells. The most common of these mutations involves the gene coding for the alpha subunit of the sarcomere protein actin (ACTC). In this form of HCM, the contracting force of the heart muscle is stronger than normal, but the heart wall thickens slowly over time. If the thickening occurs gradually, the heart may function normally for many years without causing symptoms or requiring treatment. These symptoms may occur during exercise or emotional stress, when the heart must work harder to pump blood. Erb-Duchenne palsy is also known as radial nerve palsy/paralysis. It is caused by injury to the neck which damages the radial nerve. Symptoms include loss of muscle tone in the shoulder, loss of flexion of elbow, wrist drop (unable to fully flex wrist), claw hand and loss of sensation in the middle of the dorsum of the hand. Klumpke paralysis is similar to Erb's paralysis but occurs when there is damage to the lower part of the brachial plexus. The short head of the radial nerve is most commonly affected. Symptoms include loss of muscle tone in the shoulder, loss of flexion of elbow, wrist drop (unable to fully flex wrist), claw hand, loss of sensation in the lateral side of the dorsum of the hand, numbness in the thenar eminence of the palm and pain and tingling in the thumb and lateral two and a half fingers.  Carpal tunnel syndrome is compression of the median nerve as it travels through the wrist at the carpal tunnel. Symptoms include pain, pins and needles, numbness or a tingling sensation that usually affects the whole hand. The symptoms are often worse at night and can be felt up someone's arm. Pain may be felt in the shoulder. The symptoms are often worse when flexing the wrist or gripping objects.  Claw hand is a condition where the tendons that bend the knuckles become permanently injured or cut. This means that the patient cannot flatten their hands. The condition causes deformity and stiffness in the hand. It is usually caused by injury to the upper trunk of the radial nerve. Other causes include rheumatoid arthritis and compressive neuropathies. Serotonin syndrome is the excessive serotonin levels in the brain, which can occur when too many drugs that act on the serotonin system are taken at once.  The classic triad of symptoms is changed mental status, autonomic instability and neuromuscular changes. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is different, as it is caused by dopaminergic excess. Symptoms include muscle rigidity, fever, altered consciousness and hyperactive reflexes.  Emily's medications put her at risk of developing serotonin syndrome - citalopram is an SSRI, the COCP contains ethinylestradiol and levonorgestrel, both of which have oestrogen receptors which affect serotonin levels in the brain and Piriton causes histamine release, causing vasodilation and a release of serotonin. It can also cause constipation.  The increased agitation and disorientation may be due to the serotonin syndrome, but they could also be caused by the COCP, as some women experience ADRs such as mood changes, dizziness, headaches and breast tenderness. 80% of ectopic pregnancies occur in the ampulla (where the fallopian tube is widest), 15% in the internal os & 5% in the rectouterine pouch. Ectopic pregnancy occurs when a zygote implants outside of the main cavity of the uterus, commonly in the fallopian tube. Symptoms include pain in the lower abdomen, vaginal bleeding, dizziness and syncope, loss of consciousness. Diagnosis is usually based on a combination of clinical presentation and serum beta-hCG levels. Treatment options are nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs, methotrexate or surgery. 1 in 4 women who have had one ectopic pregnancy will experience another. Risk factors are previous ectopic pregnancy, infertility, pelvic inflammatory disease, tubal surgery, endometriosis, advanced maternal age, smoking and infertility. 30% of women with an ectopic pregnancy lose the pregnancy naturally. It accounts for 6% of all pregnancy losses and 95% of extrauterine pregnancy. 10% of ectopic pregnancies result in death of mother. 10% of women who undergo laparoscopy for ectopic pregnancy develop postoperative complications including bowel obstruction, bladder injury and damage to other viscera. 1 in 5 of these patients require reoperation within 2 years. 10% of women who have undergone laparoscopy for ectopic pregnancy suffer from chronic abdominal pain. 85% of corticospinal fibres decussate at the lower part of the medulla. 15% cross over in the brainstem (pons). This means that most motor function to the contralateral side is controlled by the upper motor neurone, as the axon of the UMN decends below the point where the LMN decussates. This gives us a great deal of control over movement of the limbs. However, it also means that higher functions are more vulnerable to damage from disease and injury. For example a stroke affecting the middle cerebral artery will cause damage to the tissue supplied by this artery but also damage to the UMN decussating in the pons. Therefore the patient will lose motor function to the contralateral limbs.  Symmetrical diplegia is another example of this. This occurs when a lesion damages the anterior spinothalamic tract in the medulla. This tract carries the spinothalamic tract, and therefore sensory information from the body, and the UMN which decussate here. Therefore there is loss of motor function to the contralateral limb and sensation to the ipsilateral limb. Patients describe this as 'feeling like their legs are stuck in concrete'. Population screening tests are either 'true' or 'false'. True tests will always give a positive result in those with the condition and a negative result in those without the condition. False tests have a positive predictive value (PPV). PPV is defined as the probability that a patient with a positive screening test has the condition. For example, if a 'false' test gave a positive result in 99% of cases of cystic fibrosis, the PPV would be 99%. Screening programmes may also use tentative tests where the results are followed up by further testing. For example, it is common to use ultrasound scans to look for signs of Down's syndrome in pregnant women. This is because there is no single test that can give a definitive diagnosis of Down's syndrome. If an ultrasound scan shows possible signs then the mother may be offered diagnostic amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling (CVS). These procedures involve taking a small sample of cells from the foetus under ultrasound guidance. The cells are then analysed in the laboratory to check for chromosome abnormalities. These tests are accurate but they carry a small risk of miscarriage. Screening test results must be interpreted in conjunction with other risk factors such as maternal age. For example, although Nuchal Translucency Test (NT) has a high detection rate for Down's Syndrome, only 50% of pregnancies with a positive screen result will actually have Down's syndrome. Therefore, the positive predictive value of this test is only 50%. This means that for every 10 pregnant women who are found to have a positive NT screening result, only 5 will go on to have a baby with Down's syndrome. Neisseria Meningitidis is the causative agent of bacterial meningitis. It is a gram negative diplococcus bacteria, which causes a very severe form of bacterial meningitis. Symptoms appear 2-7 days after infection, and it requires immediate treatment with antibiotics. Dexamethasone may also be used to reduce inflammation around the brain.  Viral meningitis usually presents with milder symptoms than bacterial meningitis, and does not require immediate treatment with antibiotics.  Fungal meningits is seen in immunocompromised patients, as well as patients who have undergone neurosurgery or intravenous drug users. It is caused by Cryptococcus or Histoplasma.  Tuberculous meningitis is caused by the mycobacterium tuberculosis, and is often asymptomatic. It occurs in debilitated patients.  Streptococcus pneumoniae is the cause of a large proportion of cases of bacterial meningitis. It is often asymptomatic, but can present with neck stiffness, vomiting and photophobia. Monoamine oxidases break down tyrosine and tryptophan into their final products. However, when they are blocked, excess tyrosine and tryptophan builds up, leading to pathological side effects. Anterior cord syndrome is the most common form of spinal cord syndrome. It is characterised by a loss of pain and temperature at and below the level of injury with intact 2-point discrimination, proprioception and vibrations. There will be complete motor paralysis below the level of the lesion.  The anterior portion of the spinal cord is the most vulnerable to injury because it is surrounded by the posterior vertebral elements. The anterior spinal artery supplies blood to this portion of the spinal cord and is more susceptible to damage, leading to an anterior cord syndrome.  Central Cord Syndrome is the second most common syndrome. It occurs due to a bruising or contusion of the spinal cord (diffuse axonal injury). This causes a narrowing and a wedge shaped area of demyelination and necrosis beginning near the midline and extending down towards the periphery. It results in a loss of motion and sensation in the lower arms and hands.  Posterior cord syndrome is rare and only occurs when there is a complete transection of the dorsal columns. This would result in impaired vibration, position and proprioception sense, as well as a loss of light touch and pressure in the sacral and lumbar regions.  Brown-Sequard syndrome is a hemicord syndrome where there is a complete transection of the spinal cord. This means that there is a loss of all motor, sensory and autonomic functions on the contralateral side. On the ipsilateral side, there is a loss of pain and temperature, and partial loss of proprioception and vibration sense.  Paget's disease is a bone disorder characterized by a disorder of bone remodeling. It leads to abnormal bone architecture, and weakening of bones. It usually affects older adults and is named after Sir James Paget who described the condition in 1877. 1) Incoming calcium ions will bind to calmodulin which will then activate the phosphorylase domain of PKA. This will increase intracellular cAMP levels.2) Increased cAMP will cause a conformational change in phospholamban which will allow it to interact with RyR2.3) Calsequestrin will bind to the luminal side of the RyR2 channel acting as a voltage dependent gating mechanism.4) FKBP will bind to the cytoplasmic side of the RyR2 channel causing a conformational change which will inactivate the channel.5) Calbindin will bind to free calcium ions in the sarcoplasm preventing them from binding to troponin.   The above description explains how calcium is removed from myocytes following contraction. It is important that the RyR2 channels are inactive so that calcium ions can not exit the cell via this route. The increased cAMP will also result in increased activity of the NCX Na+/Ca2+ exchanger. This will remove calcium ions from the cell by allowing three sodium ions into the cell whilst one calcium ion leaves. This is useful when calcium ions need to be removed quickly (e.g. during each heart beat). However, it cannot remove all of the calcium ions from the cell and so the RyR2 channels must also be inactive. This is why both calbindin and calsequestrin are required to inhibit the RyR2 channel.  Binds to the luminal side of the RyR2 channel and acts as a voltage dependent gating mechanism. If the membrane potential becomes more negative, calsequestrin will bind and cause the channel to open.
